notes.meaning: Ezekiel's guide has finished showing him the temple area. Now he brings Ezekiel back to the east gate of the outer court. This is where Ezekiel will watch God arrive.

The glory of God, the bright sign of His presence, comes from the east. Years before, Ezekiel had seen it leave the temple toward the east, and now it returns the same way. God's voice is like a mighty roar of waters that carries far. His glory is so bright that the earth shines with it. This is the glory of Israel's own covenant God, not a lifeless idol made by craftsmen.

Ezekiel sees the same vision of God he saw by the River Kebar (chapter 1). He also saw it when he "came to destroy the city." That means when he announced Jerusalem's fall in God's name. God shows Himself the same way in judgment and in mercy, because He does not change. Ezekiel falls on his face, overwhelmed and worshiping.

The glory enters the temple through the east gate. It had left the old temple because of Israel's sin (chapters 10–11), and now it comes back. God may seem to leave His people for a while, but He returns with lasting kindness.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teaching links this verse to the walled-up Eastern Gate in Jerusalem today, or to Jesus' entry into the city. Others point out that this is not the gate Jesus used.

notes.meaning: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up and brings him into the inner court so he can watch. The glory of the LORD fills the temple. It fills it just as it filled the tabernacle in Moses' day and Solomon's temple. A building only truly becomes God's house when He comes to live in it.

Ezekiel hears God speaking to him from inside the temple. The "man" beside him is the guide who measured the temple (40:3). Wesley and Matthew Henry saw Christ in this man. He stands by us so we can bear to hear God's voice.

God says the temple is His throne, where He rules as King, and His footstool, where He rests among His people. He will live among Israel forever. That is something never said of the tabernacle or Solomon's temple. Israel will no longer dishonor His name by "prostitution," which means turning to idols. The "funeral offerings for their kings" is hard to explain. Some take it to mean dead, useless idols. Others take it to mean royal graves built too near the temple.

differ.view: The "forever" promise goes beyond anything said about earlier temples. It shows God is not finished with the nation of Israel and its land.
Ezekiel pictures the coming new creation in the temple language his readers knew. The vision is fully realized in Revelation 21–22.

notes.meaning: Israel's kings had set up places of idol worship right beside God's house, even in its courts. King Manasseh is one example. Only a wall stood between God and their idols. That was a bold insult to Him. So God judged them in His anger and sent them into exile.

Now Israel must put their idols far away from God and His temple. Then He will live among them forever. They had suffered for their sin, and God was returning in mercy. So they should not throw away that blessing again.

Ezekiel is to describe the temple to Israel. When they see how much mercy God has in store for them, they will feel ashamed of their sins. God's goodness is meant to lead us to repentance, which means turning away from sin. The plan also shows them the holy pattern they should have lived by.

If the people are truly sorry, Ezekiel is to show them the full design of the temple. That includes its layout, its entrances and exits, and its rules for worship. He must write it all down so they can remember it and obey it. Along with God's promised blessings, we must learn what He asks of us.

The basic law of this temple is holiness. Before, only the inner room called the "most holy place" carried that title. Now the whole area on the mountain is most holy. Matthew Henry saw here a picture of all believers drawing near to God through Jesus (Hebrews 10:19). Every one of them is called to live a holy life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read Ezekiel 38–48 as an early kind of vision writing about an ideal world, given to the exiles. On this view it cares more about ordering holy space than about real buildings.

notes.meaning: Now the altar for burnt offerings is described. It sits at the very center of worship. It is measured with a long cubit, about a handbreadth longer than the usual one. It sits in a base with a gutter and a rim around it. Matthew Henry saw this altar as pointing to Christ, "our altar."

The altar rises in steps, with ledges that get smaller toward the top. Matthew Henry pictures priests standing on these ledges. They handed the offerings up to one another to lay on the altar. In serving God we help one another.

The top part of the altar is the hearth, where the fire burned the offerings. It is four cubits high. A horn sticks up at each of its four corners. The Hebrew names here may mean "mount of God" and "hearth of God." The horns are often seen as a sign of strength.

The hearth is a perfect square, twelve cubits each way. The ledge below it is fourteen cubits square. The altar is larger than the one in Moses' tabernacle, which had to be carried from place to place. Its steps face east. The tabernacle's altar had not been allowed steps.
God gives rules for dedicating the altar on the day it is built, before regular sacrifices begin. The altars of the tabernacle and Solomon's temple were also set apart before they were used.

differ.view: This temple will be built during Christ's thousand-year reign. Its sacrifices will not forgive sin, since Christ did that once for all. They will be memorials or object lessons about sin.
The temple was never meant to be built. Its measurements are symbolic, and its worship points to Christ and the new creation.

notes.meaning: A young bull is to be given as a sin offering, a sacrifice to deal with sin. It goes to the priests of Zadok's family. Solomon had put Zadok's family in charge of the priesthood, and God now confirms it. Ezekiel gives the orders, and the priests do the work. Matthew Henry notes that Zadok's name means "righteous."

Some of the bull's blood is put on the altar's horns, corners and rim. This cleanses the altar and makes atonement for it. Here that means making it clean and fit for holy use before God. Matthew Henry points to Christ's blood, which makes both worshipers and their gifts acceptable to God.

The rest of the bull is burned in a set place inside the temple area but outside the holy sanctuary itself. Ezekiel mentions only the details that differ from the usual way of offering. He assumes readers know the rest.
On the second day a perfect male goat is offered as a sin offering. The priests cleanse the altar with it in the same way as with the bull.

After the cleansing, a perfect young bull and a perfect ram are offered as burnt offerings. A burnt offering was wholly burned and given completely to God. The priests throw salt on them. Salt stood for a lasting covenant that cannot spoil. Matthew Henry adds that grace is the "salt" that should season all our worship.

For seven days, a goat is offered each day as a sin offering, along with a young bull and a ram. The first day uses a bull for the sin offering instead. Seven days was the usual length for dedicating something in God's law. Ezekiel spells out the details so the people could follow them.

For seven days the priests make atonement for the altar and cleanse it. In this way it is set apart for God. The words used here picture filling the altar's "hand" with gifts, so it would never be empty. Matthew Henry adds that we must give ourselves to God before we serve Him.

From the eighth day on, the priests offer the people's regular burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then God says, "I will accept you." Those who give themselves to God are accepted by Him. First God accepts them, and then He accepts what they offer, through Christ.
